name: Acoustic Feature → Emotion Mapping (Bottom-Up Pathway)
short_description: Specific acoustic features (tempo, mode, loudness, timbre, register, contour) reliably predict emotional responses through bottom-up pathways; R² = 0.60-0.80 for perceived emotion; two-stage model: fast bottom-up default + slow top-down modulation
structural_pattern: Specific acoustic and musical features reliably predict emotional responses through bottom-up pathways that are partially independent of prediction error, personal memory, and aesthetic evaluation. FEATURE-EMOTION MAPPINGS: (1) Tempo (strongest predictor) — Fast >120 BPM → happy/excited/energetic; Slow <76 BPM → sad/tender/peaceful. Cross-culturally robust, present in infants. (2) Mode — Major → happy/bright; Minor → sad/dark. More culture-dependent than tempo. (3) Loudness — Loud → power/arousal/anger; Soft → tenderness/sadness/intimacy. Large dynamic contrasts → excitement/surprise/awe. (4) Timbre — Bright/sharp → excitement/aggression; Warm/soft → tenderness/sadness; Harsh/noisy → tension/anger/fear. (5) Register — High → brightness/lightness/tension; Low → darkness/gravity/power. (6) Contour — Rising → tension/excitement; Falling → resolution/sadness; Arch → completion. TWO-STAGE MODEL: Stage 1 (bottom-up, fast) — acoustic features activate B, R, C mechanisms → default emotional characterization. Stage 2 (top-down, slow) — prediction error (M), memory (E), aesthetic judgment (A) → individual modulation.
higher_order_principle: Acoustic features provide the bottom-up emotional coloring that is INDEPENDENT of prediction. A slow, minor-mode, soft passage will be perceived as sad regardless of whether specific notes were predicted or surprising. But the INTENSITY and SPECIFICITY of the emotional response depends on prediction error, personal memory, and aesthetic evaluation. Stage 1 accounts for 60-80% of perceived emotion variance (why sad music sounds different from happy music); Stage 2 accounts for individual variation (why the same piece moves one listener and not another).

tempo.mechanism: Rhythmic entrainment (R) + emotional contagion (C — resembles speech prosody)

mode.cultural_dependency: More culture-dependent than tempo; debate about spectral basis

loudness.mechanism: Brainstem reflex (B) for extreme loudness; emotional contagion (C) for dynamics

timbre.mechanism: Brainstem (roughness detection) + auditory cortex (spectral pattern categorization)

register.mechanism: Acoustic (high frequency processing) + cross-modal (spatial height association)

contour.mechanism: Parallels speech prosody patterns across languages (emotional contagion C)

regression_model.formula: Perceived_emotion = β₁(tempo) + β₂(mode) + β₃(loudness) + β₄(timbre) + β₅(register) + β₆(contour) + ε
regression_model.r2_gap: Variance explained by top-down mechanisms = difference between perceived and felt emotion models

stage_1_bottom_up.mechanisms: B (brainstem reflex), R (rhythmic entrainment), C (emotional contagion)
stage_1_bottom_up.explains: Between-piece variance (why sad music sounds different from happy music)

stage_2_top_down.explains: Between-listener variance (why same piece moves one listener but not another)

causal_links.evidence_base: Eerola & Vuoskoski (2011); Eerola et al. (2013) — regression models achieving R² = 0.60-0.80
Gap between perceived and felt emotion models; individual differences in emotional responses to same music

scope_conditions: Applies to music with identifiable acoustic features
The mappings are probabilistic, not deterministic — many counterexamples exist
Cultural calibration needed for mode (major/minor) effects
The two-stage model is theoretically motivated but not yet formally validated as process model
moderators: Musical training may shift sensitivity to different features
Individual differences affect Stage 2 modulation (empathy, absorption, openness)

interactions.nature: M17's Stage 1 implements B, R, C mechanisms; Stage 2 implements M, E, A mechanisms
M17 explains why sad music SOUNDS sad (Stage 1); M15 explains why it can FEEL pleasurable (Stage 2)
